strengths: Well-motivated technical approach with hierarchically-designed attention mechanism specifically tailored for multi-subject video generation and identity preservation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple complementary metrics (FaceSim, NexusScore, NaturalScore, GimeScore) and systematic ablation studies demonstrating component contributions
Strong empirical results showing consistent improvements across all metrics compared to state-of-the-art baselines (FaceSim: 58.12%, Text-Video Alignment: 49.55%, Total Score: 54.33%)
Valuable dataset contribution with careful curation pipeline combining OpenS2V-Nexus, synthetic data, and manual annotations for diverse multi-subject scenarios
Compelling visual results (Figure 4) demonstrating superior identity preservation and temporal consistency, especially in complex multi-subject scenes
Strong reproducibility commitment with detailed architecture specifications, implementation details in appendices, and promise to release code and pretrained models
Practical demonstration of controllable video editing applications, showing method versatility beyond generation
Clear technical presentation of hierarchical attention mechanism with three well-justified levels (intra-subject, inter-subject, multi-modal)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily an engineering contribution combining existing techniques (Rectified Flow, hierarchical attention, VLM guidance, Flow-GRPO online RL) without major fundamental advances
Critical missing computational analysis: no inference time, memory requirements, FLOPs, or efficiency comparison with baselines despite complex multi-component architecture

Evaluation lacks human judgment—no user studies validating perceptual quality, identity preservation, or temporal consistency; heavy reliance on automated metrics (NexusScore, GimeScore) without established community validation

Insufficient generalization analysis: no evaluation on unseen subjects, out-of-domain scenarios, varying video lengths, or semantically novel concepts; limited to 180 subject-text pairs for evaluation
Inadequate failure case analysis: no discussion of method limitations, struggles with >3 subjects, challenging subject types, or problematic scene compositions; cursory limitations section

Limited ablation depth: no justification for three-level attention hierarchy vs. alternatives, no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, no comparison with alternative RL approaches or simpler post-processing
Dataset scale underspecified: training dataset composition not clearly quantified; potential biases from OpenS2V-Nexus and synthetic data not discussed; unclear training-test overlap
Technical presentation gaps: architecture overview (Figure 2) overly complex; VLM integration during inference underspecified; loss weights not explicitly stated; RL training hyperparameters missing

Evaluation methodology concerns: metric combination weights in 'Total Score' not justified; impact of reference image construction strategy (Figure 9) only qualitative; no quantitative analysis of ablation gains
Baseline coverage gaps: some comparisons with 2024-2025 methods; proprietary systems (VIDU, Pika, Kling) mentioned but not compared; missing very recent multi-subject generation work from 2025

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem of multi-subject video synthesis with multiple competing constraints (identity preservation, temporal consistency, semantic alignment)
Demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple evaluation metrics compared to recent baselines (Table 1), with notable gains in FaceSim (58.12% vs 54.33% for VACO+1B) and Text-Video Alignment
Provides comprehensive system design integrating hierarchical attention, VLM-based semantic understanding, and RL refinement to handle multiple aspects of the problem
Includes substantial effort in dataset curation with 180 unique subject-text pairs, manual verification, and diverse scenario coverage across human, object, environment, and nature categories
Presents clear ablation studies (Table 2) quantifying the contribution of individual components (hierarchical attention: ~8% improvement in FaceSim)
Demonstrates practical applications (Figure 6) for controllable video editing including subject replacement and background modification
Provides qualitative results (Figures 4-5) showing visually stable identity representation and improved temporal coherence compared to baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: hierarchical attention is well-established, VLM integration for semantic understanding is increasingly standard, and Flow-GRPO is directly adapted from prior work (Liu et al., 2023). Core contribution is system-level engineering rather than novel techniques or theoretical insights

Evaluation scale is inadequate for a venue like CVPR: only 180 unique subject-text pairs is small; all examples cluster around similar scenarios (human-centric, indoor/outdoor); no cross-domain evaluation or assessment on diverse subject categories

Evaluation metrics are not validated: NexusScore, NaturalScore, and GmeScore are not well-established in the community; no human evaluation study demonstrating correlation with actual video quality; arbitrary weighting of metrics in 'Total Score'; CLIP-based metrics have known limitations

Computational cost completely unaddressed despite acknowledged 'high computational costs': no runtime comparisons, FLOP counts, or memory requirements; no efficiency analysis despite hierarchical attention + dual VLM + RL training likely adding substantial overhead

Dataset construction heavily depends on proprietary models (GPT-4o, text-to-image generators) and automated processes (DINO-based decomposition), raising reproducibility concerns; no analysis of data quality, inter-annotator agreement, or quality issues; prone to error propagation

Technical clarity insufficient: Figure 2 is overly complex; hierarchical attention mechanism lacks clear mathematical formulation and theoretical justification for why it prevents identity degradation better than alternatives; the role and integration of semantic tokens is vague

Missing critical comparisons and ablations: no comparison with simple baselines (independent single-subject generation + composition); no comparison of attention mechanism variants; baselines may not be optimized for multi-subject scenarios

No failure case analysis: no discussion of scenarios where identity is lost or temporal consistency breaks down; no analysis of when VLM-based understanding helps vs. hurts; no sensitivity analysis of design choices

Limited generalization analysis: all examples involve 1-4 subjects with similar characteristics; scalability to many subjects and highly diverse subject types unexplored; no analysis of quadratic complexity scaling of hierarchical attention with subject count

Insufficient justification for architectural choices: why hierarchical attention specifically? why this VLM over alternatives? why equal weighting of quality and identity in reward function? No ablations or sensitivity analyses provided for these critical decisions

Reproducibility concerns beyond dataset: dependency on specific model versions, complex multi-stage curation pipeline, reliance on proprietary APIs; while authors promise code release, the practical reproducibility remains questionable
Weak reference image construction justification: comparison with alternatives (Figure 9) is only qualitative; no quantitative analysis of impact of reference image quality on final video quality

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing key challenges in multi-subject video generation (identity preservation, semantic integration, temporal consistency)
Technically sound hierarchical identity-preserving attention mechanism with three progressive aggregation levels (intra-subject, inter-subject, multi-modal)
Comprehensive experimental validation showing consistent improvements across multiple metrics (FaceSim +4.93%, GimeScore +6.27%) with both quantitative and qualitative results
Thoughtful dataset contribution combining OpenS2V-Nexus, synthetic augmentation, and subject decomposition with careful construction strategy
Innovative integration of pretrained VLM for semantic understanding and online RL training phase (Flow-GRPO) for alignment refinement
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 2, 4) and well-structured paper organization
Demonstrated practical utility through controllable video editing applications (Section 4.4)
Commitment to reproducibility with promised release of code and trained models, detailed implementation specifications
weaknesses: Computational cost analysis entirely absent - no runtime comparisons, memory footprint, or inference time provided despite complex pipeline combining VAE, hierarchical attention, VLM inference, and RL training
Limited experimental scale with evaluation on only 189 unique subject-text pairs, raising concerns about generalization claims and robustness to diverse prompts

Temporal consistency claims inadequately supported - no direct temporal coherence metrics, optical flow analysis, or frame-difference validation despite temporal consistency being claimed as key contribution
Heavy VLM dependency with insufficient analysis - no ablation on VLM choice, no discussion of VLM limitations/biases, unclear robustness to pretrained model variations or unavailability

Online RL training phase overhead not justified - data requirements, training time, convergence properties, and necessity conditions not specified; adds significant complexity vs. standard fine-tuning
Generalization limited to human subjects with no evaluation on multi-subject object/animal scenarios; unclear how hierarchical attention generalizes beyond subject-centric applications
No user study validation - metric improvements cannot be confirmed to correspond to human perception preferences, limiting evidence for practical significance
Missing failure case analysis - no explicit discussion of when hierarchical attention fails, complexity limits, occlusion handling, or challenging interaction scenarios

Dataset biases not addressed - effect of significant synthetic data augmentation on real-world performance unclear, semi-manual subject decomposition risks inconsistencies, demographic/cultural biases not analyzed
Metric limitations - reliance on relatively new metrics (NexusScore, GimeScore) with limited community validation; automated metrics may not capture perceptual quality differences

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation addressing the practical challenge of preserving individual identities in multi-subject video generation while maintaining temporal consistency and quality
Thoughtfully designed hierarchical identity-preserving attention mechanism with three-stage design (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal) effectively preventing identity leakage
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines, extensive metrics, thorough ablations (Table 2), and human preference study (200 participants) confirming superiority
Substantial and consistent quantitative improvements: FaceSum 66.10% (vs 41-48%), NexusScore 45.1% (vs 39-48%), with gains across temporal consistency and visual quality
Significant dataset contribution with 218K+ masked subjects and sophisticated multi-stage curation pipeline combining OpenS2V-Nexus, synthetic generation, and human annotation
Excellent presentation with clear architectural diagrams, comprehensive appendices with implementation details (Tables S.4, S.6), and training dynamics visualization
Demonstrated practical applicability beyond generation, including zero-shot video editing capabilities (Fig. 6) showing method versatility
Clever integration of VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as semantic guide to control feature extraction and anchor generation process
weaknesses: Limited fundamental technical novelty: hierarchical attention is conceptually straightforward, VLM guidance extends prior work (Phantom), and online RL follows standard GRPO patterns from prior literature

Reproducibility challenges with complex data curation pipeline requiring cutting-edge external tools (Nano Banana, PyScene detection), in-context learning capabilities, and resource-intensive human annotation
Computational overhead of online RL phase inadequately addressed; inference time not reported; scalability with computational budget unclear
Face-specific evaluation dominance: FaceSum metric doesn't capture body/clothing consistency; multi-subject scenario details relegated to appendix; scalability with 4+ subjects unexplored

Reward design concerns: empirical weight choices (wfid=0.6, wqual=0.4) lack principled justification; ablation (Table S.7) shows conflicting metric improvements suggesting incomplete understanding of reward trade-offs
Missing justifications for design choices: why is Face-Sim appropriate for identity? Hierarchical attention configuration not ablated; online RL solution to circularity problem feels standard
Limited generalization analysis: method primarily evaluated on face-centric scenarios; full-body multi-subject performance unclear; no cross-domain or diverse demographic evaluation
Baseline comparison gaps: Phantom (2021) dated; proprietary model comparisons (VIDU, Pika, Kling) cannot be independently verified; external model dependencies (OpenV-L) could introduce bias

Technical presentation could be clearer: dense notation in Sections 3.2-3.3 lacks intuitive explanation; flow matching formulation (Eqs. 1-4) relationship unclear; some key results relegated to appendix

Incomplete failure analysis and limitations discussion: brief conclusion section; no systematic failure case exploration; potential for reward hacking or catastrophic forgetting in online RL not thoroughly analyzed

Computational overhead inadequately addressed: hierarchical attention overhead not quantified, online RL post-training cost dismissed without analysis, no inference time comparisons
